frames.narration: A noisy tenant is sending 12 jobs a second and has filled its own queue of 50. The API refuses its newest jobs with 'too many requests, retry in 10 s'. Its backlog is its own problem.

A quiet tenant submits job j-9, a report build. The API checks the tenant's own limits, which are far from reached, and puts the job on that tenant's queue. It answers 'accepted' straight away with the job's id.
A free worker takes the next job in turn from each tenant that has one waiting, so j-9 does not wait for the noisy tenant's 50. The pool has 16 workers for 16 cores, so a job gets a whole core.

The worker looks up the idempotency key for j-9 and finds none, so the job has not run. It builds the report in about 2 seconds, sends the email, and records the key in the same transaction as the result.

The worker is killed right after sending the email of another job, j-4, before it reported success. The queue's lease on j-4 runs out and another worker takes it. It finds the key for j-4, sees that the email is done, and records the result without sending again.

The age of the oldest waiting job, the noisy tenant's, passes 5 seconds. The autoscaler orders a second machine, which will be ready in about a minute. The quiet tenant's jobs never needed it: they have been served within 2 seconds all along.

A deploy starts. The first worker is told to stop: it leaves the load balancer, takes no new jobs, and finishes the two it is running. Only then does it exit and get replaced, and the next worker is stopped. The other workers carry on, so capacity never drops to zero.

A job that is still running at the end of the grace period is put back on its queue, and its key makes the rerun safe. Quiet tenants saw no failed jobs and no delay beyond a few seconds, in the middle of a flood and a deploy.
